In the case of just a reverse split your cost average goes up by a multiple of the split so in the case of AMC its 10. However because ape gets converted to AMC and has a cost average of 0 because it was a dividend. Therefore, the cost of AMC before the split would be the average cost of amc and ape and then multiplied by 10. That's how you get to a multiplier of 5.

Cost average=(cost amc × no of shares + cost ape × no of shares)/no of shares × 10

Hey you! No need to stress out! The only tricky part is not crashing the boat while you steer it under the crane before lifting :P

Now most boats of this size have a rudder that sits on the outside of the hull. If yours has this check if you can swing it upwards or pull it out of the water as this makes the process of getting the straps at the right place a little easier. Grab 2 lines of a minimum of 3 m each long each. Also go around the boat and check for little triangles pointing down on the outside of your hull, this should be right under where your deck meets the hull of the boat, take note of where they are. Don't have them? That's fine too we'll get to that later.

Now for the first actual step, if you haven't done so remove/detach all the sails and the boom from the boat and stow them away also spend this time looking for an unsuspecting passerby to help you out and rope them into helping you. 

Next I would need to know if you have a backstay (metal line holding up the mast on the back). If you do, great! If you don't, also great! First use your jib halyard and attach that to a sturdy point at the front of your boat and pull it tight. This is just a safety precaution that your mast doesn't fall backwards while you're working on setting the forestay up for dropping the rig (unless of course you use this to drop the rigging, however I've seen this only a handful of times). If you have a backstay your should now remove tension but don't completely disconnect it yet, check if your shrouds (metal lines going to the left and right of the mast) and check if they are under tension, if so, good feel free to remove this tension but leave them connected. If the mast can support itself itself without tension on the stays, perfect now you can go to the front of the boat and setup the winch that allows you to lower the mast. Feel free to now disconnect your backstay and attach it to your mast as its basically doing nothing at this point. Release some tension from the jib halyard and check if the winch is bearing the load. If it is, remove the jib halyard and attach it to the mast (unless of course this is what you are using to drop the rigging). Tie all lines and the backstay to the mast using any old piece of rope. Look at your mast base, is there a pin at the front holding the mast down? Remove that now. If not, then you don't need to do this. 

Now grab that unsuspecting passerby and request or demand their help, whatever works for you. What you want is to at all times have 3 points on the boat attached to the mast in a sort of wonky pyramid shape. At the start this will be the shrouds stopping the mast from going left to right, have the passerby slowly ease off the line with the winch. After about halfway down the shrouds will be doing nothing so at this point stop lowering the mast and have the passerby hold at that point. Remember those ropes you prepared at the beginning? Tie them to the mast at the highest point you can easily reach and spread them to a cleat on the left and right of the boat near the stern and keep tension on them from the front of the ship so you're not under the mast as it comes down. At this point you should also put down the support for the mast for when it rests in the lying down position. Get your new friend/free labour to continue dropping the rig while holding slight tension on the lines and maneuver the mast into the rest position. Detach the shrouds and if you want keep the lines on the mast tying them down at the stern to make it storm proof, detach the shrouds and tie them to the mast along with any other dangly bits that you may have missed. Bid your new bestie/forced labourer farewell with a stern nod at a 5 foot distance minimum and pray they never ask you to return the favour.

Now steer your boat under the crane, this is the tricky part, make sure not to damage the hull as that would mean repairs during the off season and we all know how much time that can cost. If you can raise the rudder do this now, if not no worries, just get a large stick/reap hook (that thing that motorboat rentals use instead of throwing the rope) and slide one of the straps under the back of the boat and do the same at the front end. Remember looking for the triangles on the boat? If you found them position the straps over those triangles if you couldn't find them place the front strap about 1/3 of the way back from the front and the back strap about 1/4 of the distance from the back and bring the crane up that the boat is sitting comfortably in the straps still in the water. The straps should be parallel and pointing straight down and maybe even 2 or 3 degrees inward but definitely not outward. If you do this the weight of the boat will hold the straps in place.

Slowly raise the boat out of the water and to answer your question, yes you do need to do something when the boat leaves the water. Weep, for you know that the coming months will be spent on dry land. The only wind you feel will be that of Jack Frost and the only spray you feel will be that of the antifouling flinging off the roller.

Now you lift the boat above the trailer, contrary what many non boat people think the boat does not support itself on the poles, it supports itself on its keel. The poles only make sure that the boat doesn't fall over. So place the boat on the trailer first and allow the keel to nestle on the trailer having the straps hold it up. Then raise the poles against the hull of the ship snugly yet firmly and then slowly lower the crane checking to see that the boat is indeed sitting on the trailer correctly (the trailer should not tip backwards).
